subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The International Space Station
description: One-minute skill: The International Space Station.

hook.text: The ISS is the largest structure humans have ever built in space—as big as a football field, orbiting at 28,000 km/h.

buildup.text: Fifteen nations collaborated to build it starting in 1998. It took over 40 missions to assemble in orbit.

discovery.text: Astronauts have lived aboard continuously since 2000. Over 3,000 experiments have been conducted in microgravity.

twist.text: It's visible to the naked eye—the third-brightest object in the night sky after the Moon and Venus.

climax.text: After 25 years of service, the ISS will be deorbited around 2030. New commercial stations are being planned to replace it.

punchline.text: Fifteen nations, one station. Humanity's home in orbit for 25 years.

quiz.question: How many nations collaborated to build the International Space Station?

details.summary: The International Space Station (ISS) has been continuously occupied since November 2000, orbiting 400 kilometers above Earth. Built by 15 nations, this football-field-sized laboratory hosts experiments in microgravity science, Earth observation, and human spaceflight that prepare astronauts for…
details.whyItMatters: The ISS demonstrates that international cooperation can achieve what no nation could alone. Twenty-plus years of continuous habitation prove humans can live and work in space long-term, paving the way for future deep space exploration.
takeaways: The ISS has been continuously occupied since November 2000
It was built by 15 nations working cooperatively in orbit
It orbits 400 km above Earth and serves as a microgravity lab

faq.question: What science is done on the ISS?
faq.answer: Experiments span biology (how microgravity affects organisms), physics (combustion, fluid dynamics), materials science (growing better crystals), Earth observation, and human physiology (bone loss, muscle atrophy, vision changes).

faq.question: What will happen when the ISS is retired?
faq.answer: NASA plans to deorbit the ISS around 2030-2031 using a controlled descent into the Pacific Ocean. Commercial space stations (from Axiom Space, Orbital Reef, and others) are being developed to replace it. The transition marks a shift from government-only to commercial low-Earth orbit operations.
